structure.title: CRediT, competing interest, data availability, references

observations.statement: The identification strategy rests on a stylized CARA mean-variance model (Section 2) yielding two numbered propositions predicting monotonic sensitivity of intermediated stocks to intermediary risk-tolerance shocks; the propositions are referenced by number when interpreting later tables.

The residualized intermediation measure is constructed so that cross-sectional variation in the sorting variable is uncorrelated with observed fundamentals, and this construction step is framed as the identifying move separating fundamental risk exposure from a pure intermediation channel.

For the S&P 500 inclusion analysis, the author explicitly names the approach a difference-in-differences estimator comparing intermediary-capital beta changes for newly included firms against several comparison groups, and states eligibility restrictions meant to avoid confounding from repeated index entry or exit.

The author argues that omitted, unobserved stock characteristics correlated with intermediary holdings would work against finding the documented pattern rather than generate it, a directional argument about the likely sign of residual confounding rather than a claim that confounding is absent.

The core sample links CRSP monthly stock returns for ordinary common shares on NYSE/Amex/Nasdaq, delisting-adjusted, to Thomson Reuters 13F institutional holdings and Compustat-derived firm characteristics, at the stock-quarter level over a stated multi-decade sample period.

Microcap stocks, low-priced shares, and financial-sector SIC codes are excluded, each justified qualitatively (trading frictions for small stocks, tradability for large institutions, endogeneity of intermediation for financial firms) rather than by one blanket data-cleaning rule.

A later mechanism section draws on a separate FactSet institutional-holdings dataset linking fund managers to bond-market positions, described as starting later and covering a shorter window than the primary Thomson Reuters sample used elsewhere in the paper.

Several inputs are described as obtained directly from other researchers rather than a public repository (a hedge-fund manager list, primary-dealer capital-shock series, systematic fund-flow shocks), indicating some non-public auxiliary datasets sit alongside the deposited replication data.

The primary sorting variable is defined as the period-by-period cross-sectional residual from regressing institutional ownership on a fixed set of firm characteristics, explicitly intended to strip out the component of holdings attributable to fundamentals before forming quintile portfolios.

The composite intermediary-shock proxy is built by standardizing two previously published shock series separately and averaging them, with a sign flip on one component justified by that source model's own theoretical prediction of an opposite-signed return relationship.

Institutional-ownership percentages and firm characteristics used to construct the sorting variable are winsorized cross-sectionally at a stated tail percentile each period to limit the influence of extreme holdings observations.

A composite conditional risk-premium control is constructed via a two-step partial least squares procedure applied to a large set of previously documented return predictors, following a cited methodology, rather than by simply averaging or summing the individual predictors.

The Fama-MacBeth characteristics table reports the time-series-averaged coefficients, an observation count, and an average cross-sectional R-squared in one compact table, with the estimating equation reproduced beneath it in the notes.

Stock-level panel tables list fixed-effects inclusion as explicit labeled rows and state the clustering dimensions and standard-error construction directly in the table notes rather than requiring readers to consult the main text.

The main stock-level panel table progresses from single-shock specifications to versions adding risk-factor interaction controls and combining multiple shock measures within one specification, a baseline-then-variants column layout repeated across several tables.

The baseline portfolio tables are built on equal-weighted quintile portfolios, a weighting choice stated and justified in the text rather than left implicit, with value-weighting introduced later only as an alternative specification.

Portfolio-level contemporaneous and predictive regressions report Newey-West standard errors using an automatic optimal-lag rule from the cited methodology, with the choice attributed to the citation rather than separately justified in prose as addressing serial correlation in overlapping quarterly returns.

The stock-level panel regressions state that standard errors are clustered by both firm and time, explaining that clustering by date addresses cross-sectional correlation while double-clustering by firm addresses additional residual correlation across observations for the same stock.

For the rolling-beta panel regression, double-clustering by stock and quarter is explicitly justified by the persistence the dependent variable inherits from overlapping rolling-window beta estimates, a distinct justification from the one given for the contemporaneous panel regressions.

The S&P 500 inclusion difference-in-differences table reports Driscoll-Kraay standard errors with a stated maximum lag length, explicitly justified by cross-sectional correlation and by overlap between estimation windows used to compute beta changes.

No discussion of multiple-hypothesis-testing adjustment appears anywhere in the text despite many coefficients being reported with significance stars across numerous quintile-portfolio and robustness specifications.

A figure plotting average characteristic quintiles over time for the top- and bottom-intermediation portfolios serves as a graphical covariate-balance check, showing spread induced in intermediation while other characteristic quintiles for the two portfolios stay close together.

Before interpreting the intermediary variable's incremental predictive power, the paper reports that the composite risk-premium control is itself a statistically robust predictor across all portfolios, used as an internal check that the control is a meaningful benchmark rather than a weak placebo.

A time-series plot of the intermediary shock variables is placed in an appendix figure and referenced from the main text specifically to support the claim that these variables are unusually volatile during the financial-crisis period.

Robustness checks reconstruct the residualized intermediation measure using both a stripped-down single-characteristic specification and an expanded set of dozens of financial ratios, then re-form and re-test the quintile portfolios under each alternative characteristic set.

Separate robustness variants value-weight the portfolios instead of equal-weighting them and exclude the 2007-2009 financial-crisis window from the sample, with results for both variants placed in appendix tables that the main text summarizes narratively.

The full robustness battery is repeated using holdings of the entire universe of 13F institutional investor types rather than only mutual funds, hedge funds, and investment advisors, to check sensitivity to the chosen institutional subset.

A separate robustness check adds stock-level illiquidity and short-interest controls to the baseline stock-level panel specification, addressing a concern raised by the paper's own reported correlations between these variables and the intermediation measure.

The intermediation sort is re-formed separately using only hedge-fund holdings, and mutual-fund/advisor holdings are further split by alignment with top- or bottom-quintile hedge-fund holdings, motivated by the hypothesis that dealer exposure concentrates in institutions closest to prime brokers.

Mutual funds and non-hedge-fund investment advisors are split by whether FactSet data currently report them as exposed to bond markets, motivated by the hypothesis that dealer intermediation in bond markets is an additional transmission channel to equity price responses.

Coefficients are consistently interpreted relative to a one-standard-deviation change in the standardized shock variable and expressed in annualized percentage-return units, a convention applied uniformly across contemporaneous, predictive, and stock-level tables.

The variance-decomposition exercise bounding the share of conditional risk-premium variation attributable to the intermediary variable is explicitly benchmarked against an analogous decomposition reported in a specific prior paper on household versus intermediary risk aversion.

Alongside point estimates, the paper repeatedly reports the associated t-statistics and describes estimates as precise or imprecise in prose, treating statistical precision as a dimension separate from economic magnitude when interpreting results.

The author notes that the discount-rate and cashflow components of returns cannot be observed separately, and frames the joint pattern of contemporaneous comovement plus return predictability as indirect, combined evidence for a discount-rate channel rather than a direct observation of it.

The author cautions that magnitude comparisons between the hedge-fund-only subsample and the broader baseline sample are not directly comparable, because the implicit comparison group of non-holding investors differs in composition across the two sorts.

Several main results are presented as coefficient plots across intermediation quintiles with shaded confidence bands, paired with a companion regression table reporting the identical specification numerically, and the plot notes state which standard-error procedure produced the bands.

Table notes consistently reproduce the numbered estimating equation beneath the table itself, in addition to stating the sample period, the standard-error type, and variable definitions, rather than relying only on in-text description of the specification.

Regression tables use a conventional multi-tier significance-star convention alongside t-statistics reported in parentheses beneath each coefficient, applied consistently across portfolio-level and stock-level specifications.

Summary statistics are split across two separate tables rather than combined into one: one reporting means and medians of portfolio-level characteristics, and a second separately reporting return moments and Sharpe ratios for the same sorted portfolios.

The introduction previews the direction and qualitative pattern of the main empirical results before the results sections appear, and closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph describing the order of the remaining numbered sections.

The paper places its theoretical model and numbered propositions (Section 2) before the data description (Section 3) and empirical design (Section 4), and subsequently references the proposition numbers directly when interpreting each empirical table.

Robustness checks are collected into a dedicated numbered subsection distinct from the main results subsections, with most of the underlying robustness tables placed in an appendix and only briefly summarized narratively in the main text.

Mechanism and alternative-explanation tests are organized into their own numbered section following the main portfolio and stock-level results, explicitly described as extending rather than replacing the baseline findings; the introduction also contains a dedicated related-literature subsection naming specific prior papers.

A dedicated Data availability section states that replication materials are posted under a named dataset title on a public data repository and gives a resolvable link, placed separately from the authorship-contribution and competing-interest statements that follow it.

The manuscript text itself does not name the statistical software used to produce the reported estimates; the estimation software is only identifiable indirectly from the deposited replication code rather than being stated in the paper.

The paper's primary inputs are commercial or subscription market and holdings databases (return data, 13F holdings, accounting characteristics) rather than survey-collected or web-scraped data, consistent with a standard secondary-data asset-pricing design.

Beyond the deposited replication data, several auxiliary series used in the analysis are described as shared directly by other researchers rather than obtained from a public database, indicating restricted, non-standard access channels for part of the empirical inputs.

A dedicated subsection adds fund-flow-based price-pressure controls from two specific prior papers to the baseline specification and reports that the coefficient of interest is essentially unaffected, explicitly framing this exercise as ruling out mutual-fund-flow-driven price pressure as an alternative explanation.

A separate liquidity-based test uses stock-level illiquidity growth, rather than returns, as the dependent variable, presented as intermediate-outcome evidence for a funding-liquidity transmission channel motivated by a cited theoretical liquidity-spiral mechanism.

In the conclusion, the author frames the equity-market estimates as a likely lower bound on the quantitative importance of intermediation frictions in other asset classes that are harder for households to access directly, an explicit claim about generalizing beyond the studied asset class.
observations.quote: lower bound on the quantitative role of intermediaries

concordance.paper_says: Stock-level panel regressions in Tables 7-8 are estimated as OLS panel regressions with stock and time fixed effects (Eq. 13-14), described as controlling for common shocks and stock-level heterogeneity.
concordance.card_shows: Card records these specs as hdfe_ols estimated via Stata reghdfe with fe=['permno','date'] (e.g. spec s1, s10-s13).

concordance.paper_says: Table 1 reports Fama-MacBeth time-series-averaged cross-sectional regression coefficients as described in Eq. (8).
concordance.card_shows: Card records this as spec s14, estimator other:fama_macbeth, implemented via Stata's xtfmb command.

concordance.paper_says: Text states that both time fixed effects (for common shocks) and stock fixed effects are included in the stock-level panel regressions.
concordance.card_shows: Card lists fe=['permno','date'] for the corresponding specs.

concordance.paper_says: Footnote states standard errors are clustered by date and double-clustered by firm for the stock-level panel regressions.
concordance.card_shows: Card records se=twoway_cluster over ['permno','date'] for these specs.

concordance.paper_says: Portfolio-level contemporaneous and predictive regressions report Newey-West standard errors with an optimal-lag rule.
concordance.card_shows: Card records se_type=hac_newey_west for the corresponding ivreg2 specs (e.g. s15-s17), using kernel(bar) bw(auto).

concordance.paper_says: The S&P 500 inclusion table states its t-statistics are based on Driscoll-Kraay standard errors with a stated maximum lag.
concordance.card_shows: Card records the same spec (s18) generically as se_type=hac_newey_west with cluster(datemo) and bw(60), without a distinct Driscoll-Kraay label.
concordance.note: Card uses a generic HAC label; paper names the specific Driscoll-Kraay procedure, but the underlying cluster+bandwidth implementation matches.

concordance.paper_says: Section 4.3 explicitly names the S&P 500 inclusion test a difference-in-differences (DID) estimator comparing beta changes before and after inclusion against comparison groups.
concordance.card_shows: Card classifies the same test under design d3 with method return_event_study rather than a DID/diff-in-diff label (spec s18).
concordance.note: Terminology mismatch: the paper's own methodological label (DID) differs from the code-trace classification (event study), although the underlying test (pre/post comparison with matched comparison groups) is the same.

concordance.paper_says: Table 6 reports six distinct named comparison groups (same size quintile, and size interacted with beta, book-to-market, profitability, investment, or momentum) as separate columns.
concordance.card_shows: Card records a single spec (s18) for the underlying regression command without enumerating the six comparison-group column variants separately.

concordance.paper_says: Text states portfolios are equal-weighted at baseline and separately reports a value-weighted robustness variant.
concordance.card_shows: Card records weights=None (null) for all listed specs, not distinguishing equal- versus value-weighting.

concordance.paper_says: Section 3 states explicit sample restrictions: share codes 10/11, NYSE/Amex/Nasdaq listing, delisting adjustment, microcap and low-price exclusion, financial-sector exclusion, and a stated sample period.
concordance.card_shows: Card's pipeline.sample_restrictions field is an empty list, not capturing these restrictions structurally.

concordance.paper_says: Table 8 (and Table 1) regressions control for profitability, CAPM beta, asset growth, book-to-market, and a size polynomial, matching the characteristic set described in Section 4.1.
concordance.card_shows: Card's spec s10 command lists control terms profit beta Gat bm lnme lnme_sq LNbe LNbe_sq, matching this description.

concordance.paper_says: Main text does not describe a graphical pre-trend check specifically for the S&P 500 inclusion event beyond the single before/after DID coefficient table.
concordance.card_shows: Card records diagnostic x1 (pretrend_plot) for design d3 with status not_found_in_scope, i.e. no pre-trend plot located in the reviewed code.

concordance.paper_says: Section 4.5 describes an extensive robustness battery (alternative characteristic sets, value-weighting, crisis exclusion, liquidity/short-interest controls, all-13F-institution sample) summarized narratively with appendix tables cited by number.
concordance.card_shows: Card's structured robustness array is empty, so none of these checks are captured as discrete robustness records.

concordance.paper_says: Section 5 describes heterogeneity splits by hedge-fund holdings and by mutual-fund bond-market exposure (Tables 9-11) presented as mechanism tests.
concordance.card_shows: Card's structured heterogeneity array is empty, so these splits are not captured as discrete heterogeneity records.

gaps: No pre-registration, IRB, or ethics statement is present; not applicable to this secondary-market asset-pricing study using standard commercial/administrative data.
The paper's own text does not name the statistical software used for estimation; Stata/SAS are only identifiable from the replication code, not from the manuscript.
No first-stage or weak-instrument statistic appears anywhere in the main text, consistent with no stage of the empirical design being presented as instrumental-variables estimation.

The Online Appendix (Tables A.1-A.9, the Appendix A model extension, and Appendix B data details) referenced throughout the main text is hosted separately via the article's supplementary-data DOI and is not included in the extracted text used for this note.
No explicit multiple-hypothesis-testing correction is discussed despite many specifications and robustness tables being reported with significance stars.

reading.note: Read the entire extracted text (introduction through references, pages 1-23) in full, including all main-text sections, table/figure notes, and footnotes. The paper's own Appendix A/B (model extension, data detail, and Tables A.1-A.9) is explicitly pointed to an online supplementary-data DOI and is not part of this text extraction, so it was not available to read; its contents are inferred only from main-text cross-references.
